lede: Sample issue, converted from AI Systems Brief Edition 20, used to test rendering. Nathan Lambert asks who will hold up the US open-model ecosystem now that Jensen Huang has left NVIDIA.

top.html: Lambert argues that open models just lost their main patron, and that compute scarcity keeps open-weight serving from becoming a commodity. If your stack leans on open weights, the supply and pricing assumptions behind it deserve a second look.
datasette-llm 0.1a11 lets Datasette's agent run on any OpenAI-compatible server. One config line moves the agent from a hosted model to one on your own machine.

articles.headline: Open-model supply loses its patron, and the economics still favor closed labs
articles.dek: Nathan Lambert reads Jensen Huang's exit from NVIDIA as a blow to US open models, and explains why compute scarcity, politics and talent make the gap hard to close.
paragraphs: In Open-source AI without Jensen, Nathan Lambert of Interconnects argues that Huang's departure matters more for the open-weight ecosystem than for GPU supply. His starting point is NVIDIA's incentive. A world with many capable open models gives NVIDIA many customers, and that keeps a handful of very large buyers from concluding that they should design their own chips. Huang acted on that incentive by funding open-model work heavily for about two years. Lambert expects the company to spend the next 24 months on stability and delivering to customers, and he expects the open-model budget to shrink.

The deeper problem, in Lambert's account, is economic. The open-model market is young, and the next few years will decide its use cases, its revenue and whether anyone has a reason to keep training new models. Its strengths so far are ownership of intelligence and enterprise post-training. But a commodity needs abundant supply, and compute is scarce. Inference startups struggle to get chips, so hosts of open-weight models face little price competition.

Politics adds a third pressure. Lambert sees growing money behind candidates who favor AI-safety regulation, many of whom regard open models as unsafe, and his nearest worry is hasty state-level rules. He expects a serious cyber incident tied to a popular open-weight model sooner or later, and notes that the most valuable open-model use happens on private infrastructure, where public data cannot show it.

His proposed fix is a true frontier open-model lab in the US. He argues the constraint is talent and scale more than money. Editorial note: these are one analyst's forecasts. The comparisons between models are his judgment, and the funding figure he cites is reported, not confirmed by the company.

figure.aria_label: Each support for US open models faces a pressure: patronage, economics, politics and frontier quality.
figure.claim: Each support for US open models faces its own pressure.
figure.caption: All rows are Lambert's argument, not measured data. Red marks the pressures he names; the teal box is his proposed answer, which he treats as uncertain.
figure.email_description: The diagram pairs four supports with the pressure on each: NVIDIA's patronage against Huang's exit; the open-model economy against scarce compute; political room against safety-backed money; frontier quality against talent concentrated in closed labs. All four lead to Lambert's proposed fix, a US frontier open lab, drawn as uncertain.

steps: List every place your stack depends on open weights and write down why: data control, cost, latency or post-training.
Keep local copies of the exact weights and tokenizer files you ship.
Make sure your eval suite can swap an open model for a closed one, so a supply or price change forces a measured switch instead of a scramble.
